newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity Magellan turned less cyclical in March.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity Magellan turned less cyclical in March.

text.p: Robert Stansky, portfolio manager of Fidelity Investments' Magellan Fund, trimmed holdings in cyclical industries in March and increased positions in growth sectors, analysts said.

"We've seen him become a little less cyclical in nature," said Eric Kobren, editor of Fidelity Insight. "That's an acknowledgement that's he's looking forward to a slowdown in the economy rather than a continued healthy clip."
Stansky did raise holdings in shares in the industrial machinery and equipment sector in March, the most recent month figures are available, but cut other cyclical sectors.

According to data appearing on the Fidelity Website, Magellan's holdings in industrial machinery and equipment rose to 8.4 percent of total assets at the end of March from 7.9 percent at the end of February, durables fell to 8.1 percent from 8.8 percent and basic industries dropped to zero from 4.2 percent. Companies in those industries in which Magellan had investments include CSX Corp and Chrysler Corp.
For the most part, investments in growth sectors rose slightly.

While investments in technology shares slipped slightly to 13.7 percent from 13.8 percent, financial stocks rose to 10.6 percent from 10.5 percent and healthcare companies rose to 7.8 percent from 7.3 percent. Magellan invested in such companies at Citicorp, Merck & Co Inc and Intel Corp in those sectors.
Energy stocks became Magellan's largest holding, accounting for 14.0 percent of assets at the end of March versus 13.1 percent at the end of February.

"He's got a big energy position and energy stocks haven't done that great the past couple of months," said Donald Dion, publisher of Fidelity Independent Advisor, a monthly newsletter covering the fund company.
Analysts said that, by and large, the fund had no significant changes over the course of the month.
"We're not seeing a lot of changes," Kobren said.
Stansky is known for less stock turnover and taking a longer-term perspective than his predecessor Jeffrey Vinik, analysts said.
